body.heading: Satellites that shout the time
paragraphs: GPS is a system of satellites orbiting Earth, operated by the United States. Each satellite carries very precise atomic clocks and constantly broadcasts a signal saying, in effect, 'I am here, and the time is exactly this.'

Your phone is only a listener. It never transmits to the satellites; it receives their signals and works out its position from them, which is why checking a map does not tell the satellites anything about you.

body.heading: Distance from timing
paragraphs: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, so your phone can calculate its distance from a satellite by measuring how long the signal took to arrive. A tiny delay means a huge distance, which is why the clocks must be so exact.

Knowing your distance from one satellite puts you somewhere on a giant sphere around it. Distances from more satellites narrow the spot down — this is called trilateration. In practice a receiver uses signals from at least four satellites, with the fourth helping to correct timing errors.

body.heading: Why it sometimes gets it wrong
paragraphs: Signals can be blocked or bounced by tall buildings, tunnels, and dense tree cover, which is why your dot on the map sometimes jumps across the street in a city centre. Weather in space and small errors in satellite positions add their own wobble.
Even so, ordinary GPS is typically accurate to within a few metres in open sky — remarkable for a system built from clocks twenty thousand kilometres overhead.

takeaway: GPS works by timing signals from satellites with atomic clocks and using trilateration to turn those timings into a position — your phone only listens, it never transmits.
